speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRESENCE OF TELEVISION CAMERAS IN FOYER-PROVISION OF OTHER SPACE
speechtext:
As hon. members are aware, television cameras have been located for some time in the foyer adjacent to the House of Commons. Propriety of this procedure has been considered by the Chair in consultation with House Leaders and with the executive of the Press Gallery. It was agreed by all concerned, in the course of these lengthy discussions covering several months, that the decision should be left with the Chair. The decision has been made that on an experimental basis, the foyer should no longer be used for this purpose. To give effect to the decision Room 110-S, located at the foot of the stairs leading to the foyer, has been made available to the Press Gallery for the purpose indicated, in addition to Room 154-D which was already available to members of the Press Gallery for radio and television interviews. Technical objections having been made to the use of this particular space, Room 238-S has also been allocated to the Press Gallery on a temporary basis for interviews following Orders of the Day.
This decision has had the effect of bringing into focus a long-standing problem, that of television and radio coverage of the House and its committee proceedings. In view of the wide interest shown in the situation, I have taken the liberty of consulting with the House Leaders and suggesting to them, as they are representative of the members of all parties in the House, that the whole issue should be considered forthwith by the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. I propose to have a further meeting with the House Leaders in the hope that a suitable reference will be made as soon as possible.
I think I should insist that in so far as I am particularly concerned, as the custodian of the dignity of the House of Commons and its proceedings, I feel as strongly as ever today that the foyer should not be used as it has in the past for the purpose of radio and television interviews. It is my hope that the House Leaders and the Committee on Procedure and Organization, in consultation with representatives of the Press Gallery, can find a solution which will be acceptable to all concerned.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NIGERIA-BIAFRA-PLANS FOR RELIEF SUPPLIES AND ADDITIONAL OBSERVERS FOLLOWING CEASE-FIRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will no doubt wish to know what steps the government is taking with regard to the rapidly changing situation in Nigeria. The latest information we have is that the Commander in Chief of the Biafran forces has ordered his troops to stop fighting and has asked General Gowon for an immediate cease-fire. The government welcomes General Gowon's statement of reassurance to the supporters of the Biafran cause. Bringing hostilities to an end in a territory like that of Eastern Nigeria inevitably results in confusion. The government hopes that General Gowon will spare no effort in maintaining the discipline of his forces and protecting the lives of all the peoples of Nigeria.
We have, at the moment, two senior officers of the Canadian Armed Forces in the area of operations as part of the International Military Observer Team. The government is offering to provide more observer personnel.
The need for relief is bound to increase very rapidly. The government considers it of first importance that outside relief activity should be co-ordinated on an international basis in co-operation with the government of Nigeria, preferably under the aegis of the Red Cross. With this in mind, we are in touch with the Nigerian government and other governments concerned with relief activities. There are considerable stocks of food and other supplies in Nigeria and neighbouring countries, including ports like Cotonou and Sao Tome. The immediate problem is to move these supplies rapidly and effectively into the areas where they are most urgently required.

January 12, 1970
Biafran Relief
Now that hostilities have ended we hope that it will be possible to open up land supply routes. We have also asked our High Commissioner in Lagos to reiterate to the Nigerian government our willingness to mount an air drop operation without delay if this is the only means whereby relatively large stocks of food can be delivered quickly to otherwise inaccessible areas.
As announced on Friday, the government is providing $500,000 to the Nigerian Red Cross, $500,000 to the Nigerian Rehabilitation Commission and $250,000 to the International Committee of the Red Cross to aid in the delivery of food and other relief operations. Immediate steps are being taken to make these funds available and the government is exploring ways in which additional funds might effectively be used. As and when it should be required, we are prepared to provide aircraft for an airlift. Canadian Armed Forces Hercules are standing by for these operations. These should be regarded as essential interim measures because, in the long run, supplies in the quantities needed must be delivered by surface transport.
To assist our High Commission to deal with a vastly increased work load and with the special requirements that will be placed upon it, we are sending a small group of experts in relief, transportation and other fields to Lagos.
I am sure that members on all sides of the House will agree with me that we must spare no effort in co-operation with other interested nations to ensure that the tragic war in Nigeria is not followed by disastrous famine and unnecessary suffering.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NIGERIA-BIAFRA-PLANS FOR RELIEF SUPPLIES AND ADDITIONAL OBSERVERS FOLLOWING CEASE-FIRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is certainly not a time for recriminations about government policy touching on this very tragic situation. Nevertheless we must say that the maladroitness and ineffectiveness of the government's policies with regard to the Nigerian-Biafran difficulty to date have created a feeling of uneasiness on the part of all those in this country who are concerned about what may happen there now. After a very bitter and bloody war there is bound to be a legacy of bitterness which one can only hope will be overcome by appropriate arrangements. There has also been a very genuine fear of genocide on the part of the Biafrans, and it is not merely confined to the Biafrans because His

Holiness the Pope and others have expressed concern about the possibility of genocide, either actively or through starvation.
The government of Canada is now offering to supply additional military observers, but the Secretary of State for External Affairs has not indicated the extent to which Canada is pressing for this; neither has he indicated acceptance of the government's proposal or where that proposal stands. It is vitally important not only that the team of observers be enlarged but that it should have freedom of movement. It should have not only the theoretical right to go to various parts of the country but the ability to get there. There has been a terrible loss of life, sir, and we must do all we can to keep any further loss of life to a minimum.
We, like the government, welcome the willingness expressed by the governments of Britain, United States, France and other countries to participate in measures to bring relief, but surely this has to be considered in its totality. The government should not simply offer to make observers available but should take the initiative to ensure that such a team is at work in the field to report on what is actually going on there. Furthermore, the relief that is needed should be in a forward position.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs stated that a lot of supplies were available nearby. Can he assure us that the supplies that are immediately required are available? For example, will additional truck transportation be required immediately to make this relief available to the various parts of the country? Is the government now using Hercules aircraft and is it doing its part to ensure that trucks are being put in a forward position to be able to respond when required?
I agree with what the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said about the importance of co-ordination. Obviously it is of vital importance; otherwise relief efforts could degenerate into chaos. The minister has said that Canada has made a proposal, but what response has the government of Canada received? Time is of the essence. It is not a matter for long discussions with the government of Nigeria and personal emissaries going to Lagos. There must not be the sort of delay there has been in the past. Time and vigour are of the essence.
We want more than just a general statement of intentions. We want to know what is going on. We need to send observers there in
January 12, 1970

adequate numbers. We need far more information than the Secretary of State for External Affairs has given us regarding the response. What is the actual state of these proposals put forward? To what extent are they being received? What action in fact is being taken? All we have heard from the Secretary of State for External Affairs are general assurances about the willingness of the government of Canada to do certain things. We want to know what is going on. We want action and not only pious declarations.
At the conclusion of the comments on the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs I will seek the unanimous consent of the House to have the House give instructions to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence with regard to the continuing surveillance of the government's program.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NIGERIA-BIAFRA-PLANS FOR RELIEF SUPPLIES AND ADDITIONAL OBSERVERS FOLLOWING CEASE-FIRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has now become clear that the military operations in Nigeria and Biafra are coming to an end, but that does not necessarily mean that the immense tragedy that has taken place there cannot be compounded and continued unless there is urgent and immediate action within a matter of hours. I want to reinforce what the Leader of the Opposition has said, that this is a question of hours, not of days or weeks. Something must be done right away.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
The present method of feeding four million people in this unhappy country by airlift has necessarily been disrupted for the time being. Many people are on a knife-edge; threatened daily and hourly by death through starvation. In these circumstances it will be necessary not only to mount a massive international effort in the long run but to use the existing facilities provided by the people who are already there, the people who are operating the feeding centres, in the short run, which means within the next day or two. I put it to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that if there was ever a need for urgent and immediate action it is now.
I wish to pay tribute on this occasion to those gallant people who fought so tenaciously for independence and survival, as they saw it, against heavy odds. I wish to pay tribute also to all those who planned, executed and carried through the magnificent, imaginative and heroic air operation which, as I said ear-
Biafran Relief
lier, has saved up to two million people from starvation despite immense hazards and difficulties. I refer to the operations under Joint Church Aid and, initially, the International Red Cross.
It seems to me the new situation imposes heavy obligations on the international community which permitted this situation to develop. There is need not only for an expanded military observer team, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs indicated, but for a substantially expanded team whose membership would not be confined to the military alone. There is an obligation on the international community to ensure that the fear of genocide does not turn into one of the tragic facts of this generation.
There is also a long term need to organize an international community which would be able to intervene even in civil wars to preserve human rights and lives. We cannot afford in this world to experience tragedies like Biafra.
In view of the large number of questions which still arise despite the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and the immense concern of the Canadian people, I shall put forward, when the occasion arises, a motion that this matter be debated further today.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NIGERIA-BIAFRA-PLANS FOR RELIEF SUPPLIES AND ADDITIONAL OBSERVERS FOLLOWING CEASE-FIRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the beginning of 1970, we have gone through very tragic hours and very dark days. The Ralliement creditiste has been calling the attention of the government to the problems of Biafra and Nigeria far the past two years.
We note, following the minister's statement, that the government can act quickly when it wants to. It is unfortunate that this action has not been taken without any political consideration, in order to prevent the starvation of Biafrans and Nigerians. The genocide of Biaf-rans is really an unfortunate event.
We cannot understand why Canada did not intervene before today. I think that love of lucre was stronger than Christian charity. Unfortunately, pressures to prevent England from selling arms to Nigeria failed. We have rendered valuable services to that country in the past and stronger pressures from us would surely have brought results.
Finally, since the tragedy is now over, I would suggest to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that we could send to Nigeria,

January 12, 1970
Biafran Relief
besides military observers, representatives of all parties of the House who could examine the problems on the scene.
If members of Parliament can attend United Nations meetings as observers, can go to Paris, to India or to any other country, why would it not be passible for representatives of each party accompanied by military observers to visit the scene of the hostilities in order to get clear and precise information about the situation and to report to the House so that the government will be in a position to take the steps necessary to eliminate misery from that part of the world.

subtopic: COMBINING OF SOCIAL WELFARE TAXES
COMBINING OF SOCIAL WELFARE TAXES
speechtext: Will the federal government consider the advisability of combining the Old Age Security Tax, Canada Pension Plan Tax, Guaranteed Income Supplement Tax in order to provide one comprehensive payment for the aged, widowed and orphaned?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COMBINING OF SOCIAL WELFARE TAXES
speechtext:
The purpose of the Old
Age Security program is to provide for Canada's senior citizens a universal flat rate pension as a base on which they can build for their retirement years. This plan is financed by a special tax on personal income, corporation income and sales. These taxes are not identified with the individuals who pay them and eligibility for the pension is not based on their payment.
The Canada Pension Plan is complementary to the Old Age Security program and is intended to provide Canadians with additional financial security through the payment of retirement, disability and survivors benefits. This is a contributory plan under which the amount of the graduated benefits paid is related to the earnings of employees and selfemployed persons.
Questions
When the Canada Pension Plan was introduced it was realized that there would be some persons who would not qualify for full benefits during the ten-year period of transition while there would be others who would not have any entitlement due to non-employment. The Guaranteed Income Supplement program was brought into being as a means of augmenting the Old Age Security pension for this group of persons. Payments are made from the Old Age Security Fund.
Since these programs are based on two different principles, namely graduated benefits and a flat rate benefit, and since the Canada Pension Plan is not operative in Quebec, which has a comparable provincial plan, it would be extremely difficult to combine them as suggested. If in the future a decision is made to effect any changes, they will be announced at the appropriate time.

subtopic: NUCLEAR RADIATION TESTING PROGRAM
NUCLEAR RADIATION TESTING PROGRAM
speechtext:
1.	Does the federal government have a program of testing the atmosphere for nuclear radiation and, if not, for what reason and, if so, how many locations are there in Canada, how often are samples taken and what is the permissible levels of fallout and has this level been reached at any time in Canada and, if so, where and what action was taken as a result?
2.	Have any studies been carried out in Canada to determine the effects of nuclear fallout on the population and, if so, what are the results and, if not, will such studies be carried out as a preventive measure for protecting Canadians from the effects of nuclear fallout?
3.	Have any studies been carried out to determine the effect of Strontium 90 entering adult bodies by food or air and, if not, for what reason and will such studies be carried out and, if so, what were the findings?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: NUCLEAR RADIATION TESTING PROGRAM
speechtext:
1. The Department of National Health and Welfare has been regularly testing the atmosphere for nuclear radiation since 1958. Samples of air particulates are collected continuously at 24 stations throughout Canada and analysed daily in Ottawa. In assessing the data, the Department of National Health and Welfare is guided by the Recommendations of the International Commission on Radiological Protection. These Recommendations identify various "permissible" levels for specific radioisotopes, but nuclear fallout may consist of mixtures of radioisotopes and its "permissible" level varies accordingly. The "permissible" level relates to conditions of continuous exposure and the Commission has recommended that, in practice, the annual average level should be used in health assessments. The annual average at all the Department's stations has remained well below the "permissible" level each year.
2.	No direct determination of the effect has been made. For a scientifically valid study, extensive data would be needed on the incidence of various diseases, both in population groups exposed to fallout and in population groups not so exposed. Sufficient data of this kind are not available in Canada.
3.	The Department of National Health and Welfare is carrying out a comprehensive program to determine the amounts of Strontium-90 entering adult bodies by food or air but it has not been able to determine directly the effect of Strontium-90 on the incidence of disease for the reason given in answer to question 2.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the situation arising out of the destruction of the Uli airport and the possibility of the collapse of Biafran resistance, to the end that Canada may play an effective role in organizing and participating in an expanded observer team in Biafra, so as to ensure that guarantees given by the federal authorities against reprisals upon Biafran personnel be fully observed, and that a massive international reucf operation be urgently organized, utilizing where possible existing relief distribution personnel, so as to minimize the widespread starvation which is imminent.

This situation is of great concern to those who are close to the heart of the international development process. The report of the Commission on International Development headed by our former Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, highlights this concern and recommends, and I quote:
-aid suppliers should devote a significant share of their research and development resources and facilities to projects specifically related to problems of developing countries.
This Commission proposes that by 1972 such expenditures should amount to 5 per cent of all public expenditures in the industrialized countries for research and development, of which at least half should be put to work in the developing countries. The United Nations Advisory Committee on the Application of Science and Technology goes further and has proposed that donors be asked to allocate 10 per cent of their research and development resources to projects of concern to lower income countries and an additional 5 per cent to help create institutional infrastructure for science and technology in these countries.
This is an area in which Canada can play an important role and it is for this purpose that we propose to establish the International Development Research Centre of Canada. This bill results from two years of careful investigation and planning by the Canadian International Development Agency with the active assistance and participation of a number of other government departments and experts outside government, particularly the Canadian universities and a number of international institutions. A great deal of care has been taken to design an instrument that will complement and supplement the work that is being carried on by others in this field. I can assure the House that Canada's initiative in creating this body is welcomed by the entire international development community.
The centre will be basically a Canadian institution with an important international dimension. The chairman and most of the members of the centre's board of governors are to be Canadian as well as the majority of its executive committee. Both the board and the staff will include specially qualified people from various parts of the world, including the developing countries. The centre will be structured so as to provide the best possible environment for creativity and problem solving.

International Development Research Centre
The centre will identify, initiate and encourage, support and undertake research into the problems involved in the development of economically deprived regions of the world. It will seek to develop the most effective application of the results of this research to the needs of the people of those regions. It will give high priority to programs that assist the developing countries to build their own scientific and technological capabilities so that they will not be mere welfare recipients, but contributors in their own right to the solution of their own problems.
I have said that the centre will be "problem oriented". A small expert headquarters group will identify specific development problems and develop programs designed to focus resources upon them. In the development and implementation of its programs the centre would work closely with other government departments and non-governmental institutions, particularly Canadian universities and industry. A typical project might consist of a number of programs carried out on a decentralized basis by institutions and individuals chosen for their specific capacity. The centre will also be able to provide financial support to specific research activities of other institutions that contribute directly to its own programs and objectives.

For example, a program designed to improve the protein content of cereal grains might be spearheaded by a Canadian university with special experience in that field. It would involve a number of other Canadian and non-Canadian organizations, each of which would be engaged in a specific aspect of the work as part of a co-ordinated program. Appropriate authorities in the less developed countries would be involved in the crucial work of applying and adapting the results of all the work to the environmental and social conditions of those countries.
After a project has been undertaken, the function of the headquarters group will be to oversee the programs and to audit and disseminate their results. Discussions with the OECD Development Centre, the United Nations and some of the United Nations Specialized Agencies indicate that the centre's headquarters might also provide a centralized system for assimilating, storing, retrieving and disseminating scientific and technical data relevant to international development. In this way the centre would help provide an

It is too early to be specific about the centre's programs, but emphasis will certainly be given to those problems to which Canadian capabilities seem especially applicable. Final decisions on program priorities will be reserved to the centre's board of governors. CIDA and the United Nations Advisory Committee on the Application of Science and Technology to Development have already indicated several possible areas of special interest: the development of new techniques for identifying and evaluating mineral resources, improved methods of preserving food and reducing waste; the development of genetically improved plants of high protein value; the study of some specific aspects of the world population problem; and the development of efficient, labour-intensive industrial techniques.
Most of the problems with which the centre will deal will require co-operative effort by both the physical and social sciences. The very nature of the development process requires that the special skills and perspectives of the engineer, the physicist and the chemist be harmonized with those of the economist, the sociologist and the anthropologist. The centre will be concerned with the application of science and technology to the effort to improve the quality of life, not only the processes of material production.
We should not overlook the important benefits the centre will bring to Canada. The funds provided for its support will be an addition to the funds normally available for Canadian research and development. It will create new opportunities for the use of Canadian human and institutional resources in the field of science and technology. It will help to attract to Canada highly qualified people in various fields, including Canadians who have had to leave Canada to pursue their special interests. It will also help to keep in Canada some who might otherwise leave.
In all its programs, the centre will provide important linkages between Canadian and foreign science and technology, enabling Canadian specialists to obtain international experience which could make a valuable contribution to our own development.
The funds needed to finance the centre's operations and programs will come out of Canada's international development assistance allocations. Within these allocations the

amount of funds made available to the centre will depend upon the specific programs and activities which are developed by the centre's board and management after it is established. The government intends to give priority to this aspect of our international development program and I foresee the allocation of as much as 5 per cent of our total development aid funds to the centre. The government is prepared to allocate a minimum of $30 million for the administration and programs of the centre over the first five years. About one-third of this would be for the headquarters operations and the remainder for programs to be carried out outside headquarters.
Successful operation of the centre will call for the full co-operation of the Canadian scientific and technological communities and an especially close relationship with Canadian universities. The science secretariat, other departments of the federal government directly concerned with science and technology and the university community, have contributed to the studies leading to the proposal for the establishment of the centre; they will be equally involved in its direction and operation. The proposed legislation provides for this.
I am sure hon. members will agree with me that the passage of the bill to establish the International Development Research Centre of Canada will provide Canada with a unique opportunity to make an exciting and worthwhile contribution to the cause of international development while enlarging the horizons and enriching the experience of Canadian science.

We in the Official Opposition are happy that the responsibility is to lie with the hon. gentleman. If a more imaginative proposal were to be forthcoming, it might be that authority should rest with a new minister for international development, and perhaps we shall see the establishment of such a post in this country before long.
The original hopes for rapid economic progress in the developing countries have been only partially and spottily achieved. We know this to be a fact, regardless of which party we support. There will, of course, be other opportunities to discuss the uncertain record in this

field as well as Canada's external aid program. Today we are dealing with one method which the government has proposed, namely, the establishment of an international research and development centre in Canada.
The Official Opposition welcomes this bill. We shall deal with it, hopefully, in a constructive as well as in a critical manner. We intend to offer a series of amendments which we hope will commend themselves as being sensible and worthy of adoption.
It used to be part of the doctrine connected with the development of emerging nations that economic growth was just a matter of time-that the process was an inevitable one. The harsh fact is that since the end of the second world war no new country has joined the ranks of the wealthy and advanced nations of the world. This is despite a good deal of energy,, a massive injection of capital and, I would say, a considerable amount of goodwill. There are three crucial questions which must be asked about the proposed research centre; they were posed for us at a meeting of a sub-committee of the Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, the sub-Committee on International Development, by Professor Irving Brecher of McGill. They are:
1.	Is there a basic need for the agency?
2.	Has Canada the capacity to carry through the projects envisaged for the centre?
3.	What kind of results can Canadians expect?
To answer the last question first, and in a general way, I would say that Canadians cannot expect any quick results. This is, of course, one of the problems of our epoch, it seems to me-the epoch of instant coffee, instant answers, instant results. I suspect it will not be in the next five years or even in the next decade that the results of the research projects shared with the world through this research centre will make themselves felt in the poorer countries. We do not need to be reminded of the veritable maze of organizations already dealing with development problems around the globe. There is a jungle of alphabets in the international development field. I do not think we need worry about this as long as there are well defined trails through it.

It seems to me we have learned a good deal in the past few years about development aid. We have learned that we cannot superimpose on others, as we used to think we could, our

In fact, this used to be the rationalization for aid in the early years before the introduction of that great project, the Colombo plan. We have learned that ways of doing things, which may be perfectly acceptable to Canada, are not necessarily wise or valid in other countries that are at a different stage of development and which have divergent histories and a variety of cultures. We have also learned-and this seems to me the core of wisdom-that we need to know a great deal more, that we require a vast amount of research in the field. We have, as the minister said, no real focus yet upon the provision of external aid.
Another thing we have learned is that a good many organizations, including those that are adjuncts to the United Nations itself, are hidebound by outmoded procedures. The Secretary of State for External Affairs reminded us of this when he spoke to the United Nations during the 24th General Assembly.
Just as an aside, may I say that the jargon in the field of external aid has evolved during the years. It seems to me that we have now a rather more hopeful set of words which are clearer than most others-"external aid".
In the 20 years since the inception of the external aid program, the underlying motives have shifted considerably. With the research centre in operation, and with the studies that have been commissioned during the past couple of years by the welter of agencies now involved in this field throughout the world, we can surely expect to be in a better position to give aid and to understand the consequences to be expected from the giving of aid.
As we abandon the old certainties-not a unique happening these days since we are abandoning certainties everywhere, much to the benefit of mankind, I think-we come to see that it is not a question of promoting this or that political philosophy; that it is not a matter of expecting, in a sort of selfish way, some long range economic reward because we have been good fellows and extended aid; that it is not even that we can expect these results to flow within a measurable time, by which I mean five or ten years. Rather it is that the goals are much clearer now, and they are clearer because the premise on which those goals were based has been simplified. I suggest we are arriving at the point where we recognize that external aid has but one focal point-the development in the world of the poor countries.

Mr. Speaker, I begin my remarks on second reading of Bill C-12 by agreeing with the minister and with the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) that the proposal in the bill is a useful and imaginative one and that the research centre could be, and I hope will be, of immense value in the development of the most useful methods of giving aid to the developing countries of the world and the most useful methods for those countries to make use of the aid made available.
I wish to express some concern I have about the philosophical approach to the problem of international development and international aid. In doing so, I want to make clear that I am not carping critically in respect of the proposal but am trying to get the minister and his colleagues, and indeed myself and my colleagues, to look at the problem of international development in what I think might per-haos be the more appropriate context in 1970.
Paul Hoffman is reported to have said at some point that it is wrong to speak of giving international aid. One does not give international aid. The proper way to express the situation is to talk about the developing countries receiving aid and not the developed countries just handing it out to them. This is the first problem I have in respect of the suggestions in this bill and the speech introducing it made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp). It seemed to me that all the time he was speaking in the usual terms used by statesmen of developed countries concerning international development; that is-and I hope I am not doing him an injustice-we, a developed western nation having all the scientific and technical knowhow, are going to provide a research centre

in our capital that will involve Canadians in certain elements and areas of research and that we will provide the facilities for the developing countries to use if we can arrange with them for such use. In other words-and again I say I am not carping about this but am worried about it-we appear to be saying that we a rich, developed and knowhow nation will hand out to you, the poor ignorant developing nations which do not have it, all the wisdom we have and all the great things we have accepted in our kind of society.
My study of the subject, Mr. Speaker, which naturally has been as limited as that of any other member, has convinced me that when we speak in the field of international development we are wrong if we speak merely of scientific and technological matters, if we speak merely in terms of providing the developing nations with technical knowhow and the application in their countries of methods which may or may not be suitable for them, and if we speak of introducing into their societies a culture which they may or may not want introduced into their societies.

Precisely, but how can this be done with a board when, as I believe he said himself if I heard him correctly, the headquarters group would decide the priorities or the areas, whatever the term he used was, in respect of the research to be undertaken. Who is to be included in this headquarters group? We see in the bill that the board of directors must be composed of a majority of Canadians, 11 out of the 19 or 21, whichever the figure is. We find that the executive committee must consist of a majority of Canadians. There are other proposals of that sort.
I appreciate it is difficult to sell to people the idea that there is a need for international aid when it would cost the people money. This involves taking out of the production in Canada a certain amount in order to assist people elsewhere and it is necessary to persuade the Canadian constituency that this is a worth-while thing to do. My own personal experience with my fellow Canadians has persuaded me for many years that Canadians are ready to make this kind of offer to people who need assistance and are ready to make the kind of sacrifice involved if they are informed about what is being done and are
International Development Research Centre informed about the purposes to be served by international aid.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I have personally, therefore, no worry about persuading the Canadian people to support an appropriate and imaginative program of assistance to developing countries to develop themselves. Therefore, I ask why the emphasis on having a majority of Canadians? What worries me, Mr. Speaker, is this: if you have a board of directors a majority of whose members must be Canadian then you will have some others, and in that case who are the others going to be?
If I remember correctly there is a total of 21 members. There is a chairman, a president, and not more than 19 others, and of this total of 21 a minimum of 11 must be Canadian. Who are the other 10 likely to be? I bet that of the other 10 there will be someone from the United States, someone from the United Kingdom, someone from the Netherlands and someone from France. In other words, in addition to the 11 Canadians there will be a number of other representatives or citizens of developed countries.
The hon. member for Fundy Royal says that he wants at least five members of the board to be from the developing countries. Why only five, Mr. Speaker? I want to emphasize that I am not playing the numbers game. I am saying to members of this House and through you, Sir, to everyone concerned, that in my estimation, after some considerable study and thought, the developing countries ought to have a full say in the kind of research that takes place which is supposed to serve their needs.
This is not only a matter of science and technology. It is a matter of the infrastructure that must be built in these developing countries-the educational facilities, the health facilites,, the roads and all the other things that support a modern society. It is a matter of fitting into the culture of developing nations, their system of government, the desire they have and the objectives which they have for the future of themselves and their peoples. Who is going to determine that? A group of Canadians and citizens of other developed countries will have a majority say in this centre, and they will decide the priorities and the areas of research that are to be undertaken.
I am concerned about that. I am worried about it. I do not see the need for insisting that there be a majority of Canadians, and I

I am convinced that this cannot be done in the proper atmosphere and in the proper context if it is handed to the developing nations as a decision of a group of men representing mainly the developed countries of the world, which is what the bill now proposes.
Perhaps when the bill is before our committee some explanation will be given as to why we must have a majority of Canadians at every stage. At the moment I do not see it. In fact I see very great disadvantage, as I have indicated, in making the board and the centre mainly representative of the developed countries, once again telling the developing nations what they ought to have, instead of the developing nations having a full voice in what is to be done on their behalf and for their needs by this centre.
This is the first worry I have because if the plan is not implemented in an imaginative way, this research centre will simply be a duplication of research done in the United States, in Europe, and elsewhere throughout the world.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, without belittling the effort which the minister has placed before us today, I would like to indicate that I have some doubts as to whether this is the best way in which to set up research for the developing countries, and whether the better way is not to set it up inside those countries, or inside regions of those countries, rather than in Canada. I say this tentatively, Mr. Speaker. I can be persuaded that I am wrong about this, but I notice in the "Partners in Development" report of the Pearson Commission there is great emphasis laid throughout the book, and particularly at page 207, on the need for goal-oriented research in regional and national areas of the developing nations, that there ought to be regional or national laboratories and research institutes to study techniques of natural resource utilization and to make other improvements in the developing nations, and that there ought to be nationally based corporations for the purpose of developing products and processes in the developing areas.

It seems to me there is an obvious advantage in having this done in Asia, in Africa and in South America rather than in Canada. It seems to me there is an obvious advantage in having the research institute located in the area that is going to make use of the results of the research, so that the nations in the area, the representatives of the peoples of the area, can have a say in the field of research, the areas of research, the subjects of research, and the objectives of the research that will be undertaken.
You can do the same kind of thing, or at least you can assist that sort of development by a research institute located in Canada if the developing nations are given adequate representation on the board and on the executive which is to make the choice of research subjects and research areas. But when they are given only token representation the situation will be a different one.
I am worried about that because I notice that even the Pearson Commission, if I remember correctly, had only one or at most two members from developing countries. One was W. Arthur Lewis from the Caribbean countries. There may have been one Latin American person. I cannot remember where Campos was from, but most of the others were very fine people, extremely intelligent and competent in their areas but, as I say, most of them were from developed nations. I do not know why that was needed-

I thank the minister. I was going to make that suggestion myself, as to why the commission had this overweight of developed nations. In my opinion, the other reason was that it was an organization set up by the World Bank, and in my humble opinion the World Bank's approach to international development has been a disastrous one, concerned primarily with the superiority of the developed countries, concerned mainly with supporting development in developing countries which seemed to the bankers to be desirable and necessary, but which may not at all have been what the local governments
January 12, 1970	COMMONS DEBATES	2259
and the local people considered necessary and desirable. This World Bank approach was partly responsible for the choice of the commissioners, although I hasten to say that the report they produced was one of very great value.
I have emphasized this concern, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps I have belaboured it. At the moment, although I am subject to persuasion by the minister and his assistants, I am personally very unhappy about the composition of the membership and leadership of the centre, the board and executive of the centre, which inevitably will mean mere token representation from the developing countries, so that again we will have an international undertaking by the developed nations-in this case Canada and its associates-to tell the developed countries what in our view they ought to have. More and more in the last number of years, Mr. Speaker, I suggest there has been evidence that the developing countries resent this approach and personally I sympathize with their resentment. When one visits the United Nations and listens to delegates of developing countries speak officially, and when one chats with them unofficially, more and more is there evidence that they resent the notion that the developed countries are going to have control of the methods and processes and goals of their development, which is what has happened to date.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I say to the minister that there is not very much difference between what he has proposed in his bill and in his speech this afternoon and the whole, in my opinion, ill-advised concept of tied aid which we have had up to now. This is another form of tied aid and the entire developing world has protested against this notion that when a government gives assistance to a developing country, then X per cent of that assistance must come in the form of goods produced in the donor country. In its report the Pearson Commission uses a great deal of space criticizing the tied aid idea and pleading with the donor countries to drop it.
In a sense, this research centre is a tied aid notion. It was significant that the minister emphasized the fact that the centre was going to give Canadians an opportunity to have certain experience, was going to promote research in Canada. In other words, they were going to use Canadian products and Canadian goods in the sense in which international assistance is tied in the normal way. That is not the objective that the minister and his
International Development Research Centre advisers ought to have for the international research centre.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I am concerned that this centre should be merely a source of funds for research projects for universities, and which would have been carried on anyway if the centre were not available, except that there will now be another source of funds to which the universities will be able to go to promote research projects that members of their staff or post graduate students have set for themselves. That is not the purpose of the centre. If assistance for research in our universities is to be given, let it come from the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) and not from the Secretary of State for External Affairs; let it come from the Home Office; let it come from the Canada Council; let it come from whatever other source we may have for assisting research in our universities and for the development of our research and our universities. That surely is not the purpose of this international research centre, I am sure the minister would be the first to agree.
I am not therefore concerned, and I ask the minister that he not be concerned, with promoting research in our universities, with the development of Canadian research. Certainly, we will have a by-product, as will have every other country in the world, from any research carried on in this increasingly important field, but that is not the purpose. It worries me that the minister should have emphasized that because again we will have an emphasis on the things we want to do that we may think of value in promoting Canadian research, rather than an emphasis on what developing countries may require or think they require.
I agree fully with the hon. member for Fundy-Royal who spoke ahead of me. I want to support him without any reservation on the need to make absolutely clear that this research centre will have nothing to do with any military research, defensive or offensive. I am a little fed up anyway with this distinction made between defensive and offensive research. We should have nothing to do with any kind of research related to military activity in developing or developed nations,, and we must make that clear. We must make it clear by the necessary provision in the bill, later to become an act, where the powers of the board or the centre are set out. We must underline that no research in military matters will be undertaken directly by the centre or indirectly by financing any such research in the universities or elsewhere.

I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the minister will reconsider the personnel of the leadership of this centre and open it up to people of developing countries to a larger extent than can now be possible. They should be on the board and have something to say about the choice of research subjects.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I have said on many occasions and so have other members, that any law and any institution can be reduced in value-and I am picking words carefully-if the people chosen to administer that law or run that institution are not the right people. In my study of history I learned that more good laws have been perverted by bad administration than by the Parliaments that passed them. Therefore the personnel chosen for the positions of President, Chairman, Vice-Chairman and other leaders of the centre are of immense importance.
There have been occasions, Mr. Speaker,- and I cannot help saying this though I hope I have a benign smile on my face as I do- when people have been chosen for positions of importance because they were defeated in a prior election. There have been such occasions.

[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
What I am emphasizing and pleading for is that when the heads of this institute are appointed, the minister makes certain that they are people who themselves have had personal experience in the field of international aid and development. This ought not to be an academic exercise, but an exercise in practical, realistic, international co-operation and development. And if that is to come about you must have people who have lived with the peoples in the developing areas, who have a sense of their attitudes and desires and some understanding of how they think, act and react. What is done must be of the greatest use to the developing peoples of the world in order that the developing countries may have full confidence in the research institute and not consider it as just another bit of North American largesse which they distrust. It is because Canada can do this without awakening distrust that I greet the bill and the imaginative ideas contained in it. If this kind of institute is to be set up by a developed nation on its own soil, then I submit Canada is one of the few countries that can do so without arousing the fears and distrust of the developing countries.
A great deal has been written about the motivation behind international aid. Many kinds of motivation have been suggested. Some people are motivated on purely political grounds; they think international aid will help the world go in the direction in which they want it to go. I think they are blind and deaf, and quite possibly dumb. No international aid will affect the historical development of the various continents of the world unless and except that international aid helps the developing countries to develop in the direction they have decided to go. There are other people who say that international aid is necessary if we are to assure peace in the

world. This, surely, is obvious. It is surely obvious that hunger, disease and ignorance across many parts of the world are a great threat to the peace and order of the world.
There are some who say that international development is good because it will assure the developed countries of future economic growth. That is also true, Mr. Speaker, and one need not be ashamed of emphasizing the fact, because it is a fact, that the future prosperity of the people in the developed countries depends on developing prosperity in the presently undeveloped areas of the world. If at the end of 25, 30 or 40 years from now the poverty of two-thirds of the world remains as deep as now, the welfare and standard of living of the developed parts of the world will undoubtedly suffer.
Finally, there is the sheer motivation on grounds of humanity, the motivation of people wanting to help other people in need. I am not ashamed to accept that as a perfectly proper motive for the giving of imaginative and effective assistance to the needy peoples of the world. We ought not to apologize for feeling that morally we are brother's keeper, whether he is in Africa, Asia, Latin America, or here, on Canadian soil. We shouldn't feel embarrassed to admit that we are anxious to deal in a humane way with great international human problems and it should not be necessary for the minister or anyone else to emphasize Canada's advantage in this undertaking rather than the sheer, decent, civilized humanity which must impel us to help people who now suffer unnecessary want to overcome their degrading and depressing condition. These are good reasons for Canada's playing a much bigger role in international development than it has played until now. All these are perfectly good reasons why this measure should be supported by all sections of the House. I hope that when the bill comes before the committee the minister and his advisers will be prepared to accept suggestions for change which may improve the bill and improve the centre when it starts operations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House is now discussing the bill to establish the International Development Research Centre of Canada.
After reading this bill, I have come to the conclusion that it is intended to establish some sort of corporation under the direction of a board of governors.
International Development Research Centre
Secondly, under this bill, we would make available to the Centre the sum of $1 million to help them begin their research activities.
Mr. Speaker, this bill is of the greatest interest, and I wish to congratulate the minister on presenting the bill, because, as the previous speaker said, it shows great imagination as well as a desire to improve Canadian aid to developing countries.
It seems that the minister and his officials interested in Canadian aid to developing countries are trying to find new methods.
On the other hand, one should not be overenthusiastic as Canada is still in search of a policy. The actual aid given by Canada to developing countries since it joined the Colombo plan has often been inefficient.
Although Canada is an extremely wealthy and highly industrialized country, Canadians have voiced well founded criticisms of the government aid to developing countries. Canadians are perhaps right in asking their government for increased and gratuitous aid.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian policy concerns not only the members of this House but also our fellow-citizens, who do not only contribute to Canada's production and expansion, but also express their opinions unhesitatingly. And to support my views, I have here a letter from Father Fernand Noel, from Victoriaville, which I would like to quote:
I would ask you earnestly to intervene in the House so that Canada's efforts in favour of the developing countries may be intensified. It is not necessary for me to make a statement to suport my request. I rely on you.
Mr. Speaker, that Canadian feels there is no need for him to give his opinion, as he considers that Canadian aid is necessary anyway although it is definitely inadequate.
I have here a letter signed by Mrs. Germain St-Pierre, 180 Notre-Dame Street West, Victoriaville, who says, and I quote:
I have read in a newspaper your wishes for this New Year.
And particularly your wishes for peace among men and between alien countries and for the development of underdeveloped countries as well.
-I dare hope that you will use your influence with the government to promote a more equitable distribution of the funds allotted to developing countries as compared with the appropriations assigned to arms.
I rely on your support.
I could also read a letter written by Mr. Fernand Turcotte-Dostie, 24 Onil St., Victoriaville, in which he expresses his views on world peace and on the problems of developing countries, and points out that affluent
January 12, 1970
2262	COMMONS DEBATES
International Development Research Centre countries are asking themselves questions on the assistance they must extend to them while two-thirds of the world is dying from hunger.
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of boring the House by reading other letters of this nature. I did read a few because I wanted to show that Canadians living in urban or rural areas take great interest in these problems and ask that the government take measures designed to solve them immediately. In that respect, Bill C-12-I am glad to say-seems to drive the first stake in the search for an answer to requests by Canadians.
This bill provides for the establishment of a centre for research aimed at determining the value and effectiveness of our assistance to developing countries. I must say, repeat or suggest that this research centre must be more than the faithful echo of the government's voice, but rather-and that is our hope-its conscience as regards external aid policy.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
We want the Centre to make suggestions without taking the government policy into account. We want it to be, so to speak, free from instructions emanating from the Minister of External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) or any other Cabinet member, and to engage in serious, intensive research, using facilities available in each of the countries involved. The Centre should, in fact, serve as the conscience *of our present policy and a source of information for the government.
Now and always, Canadian policy in this held has been a believe-or-else policy, in short a policy of coercion.
And although Canadians wonder about it, nobody demonstrates to the government its lack of efficiency.
We hope that this centre will help to demonstrate the lack of efficiency of the government policy in connection with the developing countries so as to oblige us to improve it all the time and render it more efficient and see that it really reaches its goal.
Since Canada is one of the best industrialized countries in the world and although a certain amount of poverty exists here, we must be keenly interested in the poor countries. Canada must also devote its efforts to research. That is why we welcome the introduction of this bill.
Finally, in this same context of aid to developing countries, Canada must increase its

financial, human and technical aid to these countries.
The Canadian policy must be restated, and we hope that this centre will give the government an opportunity to do so.
Canada should try to eliminate the exploitation factors in the developing countries. I shall give here an example which is a real scandal and I should like to suggest to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that he take note of it, so as to become aware of the contradiction contained in his own policy.
Mr. Speaker, on the one hand, primary responsibility for the tragic situation in Biafra and Nigeria lies with the countries that supply arms to the belligerents and that manufacture weapons. With regard to this, Canada has done nothing. As a matter of fact, this afternoon, during the question period, I asked the minister whether he intended at least to ask that there be an investigation into this by the United Nations. He answered that no problem existed and that those responsible for the hardship and poverty of certain countries were not those thought to be so.
Mr. Speaker, that is nonsense. One knows very well that those who supply arms have an interest in keeping those countries in poverty and hardship in order to be able to exploit them better.
The Canadian policy is inconsistent in this respect and only throws dust in the eyes. On the one hand, we would like to increase our aid up to 1 per cent of our estimates, which is insufficient, and on the other, we become the accomplices of those who take unfair advantage of the poor countries until there is bloodshed.
Mr. Speaker, it seems that we should be logical and reconsider our external aid policy, so that it would not be inconsistent.
In the United Nations, Canada has not taken any valid stand against the countries which provide arms to the belligerents and keep alive the ferments of war for the sole purpose of making a profit even if harmless victims must die.
I was talking about Biafra and Nigeria. The latter is precisely a developing country. I could also talk about Viet Nam which is another developing country. We know that many arms suppliers and financiers make money through the sale of arms and other destructive devices to those countries. Canada, the United States, England and other rich and industrialized nations promote destruction and the spreading of poverty.

Such a situation seems absurd to me and it shows the inconsistency of our external affairs policy.
I would not want to delay uselessly the business of the House. The previous speakers have sized up the present situation rather well. However, I want to emphasize that the minister should see to it that this Centre is independent from political parties, in order to really be the conscience of Canada in its foreign aid policy. Through the creation of this Centre, it is proposed to the government and to the Members of Parliament to make a review of our policy, namely, to continually assess our investments. Canada should not impose its aid on any country. It goes without saying that we must make this recommendation, because if Canada imposes its views, various conflicts will result. In this connection, let us remember the failure of the American policy.
The present aid of Canada is ridiculous. We shall never repeat it enough. It is high time that Canada, in addition to founding new research centres, should increase its financial, human and technical investments. When reading the reports of development agencies, it does not take long to realize that Canada is a country which cannot boast of the aid granted to developing countries.
It is already scandalous to note that two thirds of mankind are starving. Poverty, starvation, illness and ignorance prevail. It is unfortunate to note that owing to our nonparticipation policy regarding conflicts such as those in Nigeria, in Viet Nam, etc., we help widen the gap between the affluent countries and the poor countries that we want to assist.
Such a contradiction, I feel, should be recognized by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and his officials. The establishment of this new Research Centre should have priority. The Centre will suggest a global policy to the government, enabling it to dissipate the present scandal. So, Canada might really reach a top place among countries providing foreign aid.
At the present time, we can draw great lessons from the achievements of several other countries. I have here before me the September 1968 issue of the publication entitled International Development. Canadians will not find in it any reason to be proud of themselves. That publication shows the shameful shallowness of the Canadian policy. Indeed, it is again the consequence of its inconsistency. I therefore want to insist strongly on that point. Besides, it is the only
Business of the House
one I want to rise now because I do not care to delay the debate needlessly. And once more I urge the minister to revise our external aid policy, in the light of his external affairs policy, so that we do not build on the one hand and destroy on the other but rather see to it that our country leads the way without expecting any return in order to eliminate poverty and hardships in two thirds of the world. We have in Canada, according to the minister, surpluses of wheat, of milk and of many other products still to be sold because the government is incapable of selling them. Those goods keep accumulating, while there is growing poverty in Canada, and two thirds of the world's population is starving to death.
Mr. Speaker, this should weigh heavily on the consciences of Canadians. That explains the intervention of my fellow-citizens of Vic-toriaville, in the riding of Lotbiniere, who have asked me to urge the minister to revise that policy. Indeed, Canadians would be proud to increase their help to co-operate with the minister, and to tighten their belts, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has asked, provided it really helped to check poverty and hardship. Otherwise, this is nothing but a farce, and a lack of responsibility.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT RESEARCH CENTRE
speechtext:
should like to say a few words on this bill to establish an International Development Research Centre in Canada.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the minister for bringing forward this imaginative and constructive piece of legislation, the forerunner of its kind in this field of international affairs. I think the minister would support me if I were to extend my compliments also to Mr. Maurice Strong and to his righthand man, Dr. Peters, both of whom have done outstanding work behind the scenes in connection with this legislation. They are two men who are very well qualified indeed for the positions they hold.
This bill establishes a more efficient means of expending money under what used to be known as our foreign aid plan. Many countries, including Canada, have in the past allocated a great deal of money to assisting under-developed and developing countries without really placing a great deal of emphasis upon the efficiency with which the money was being used. This is understandable; it is difficult to tell other people how to spend money once they have it in their hands, especially at the international level. The bill now before us establishes a system which enables a research centre in Canada to find the best means of solving problems experienced by the countries to which we are providing assistance. It is necessary, of course, that this research organization should not become too centralized. If it is to provide information covering many different types of industry in developing countries having widely different needs, it is self-evident that the necessary research cannot be carried on in any one centre in this country.
The central proposal in this bill is that we should set up an international development research centre which is to be problem-oriented, and much of the work to be done will
January 12, 1970

find its way to other research institutions and other areas of Canada. This is as it should be. Personally, I should not want to see the establishment of an organization which is too strongly orientated toward the universities. In the past we have depended to a large degree upon university staffs for research, ignoring the fact that we have a wealth of scientific knowledge and experience at our disposal in industry and in many of the Crown corporations of Canada-a wealth of scientific staff who are not directly concerned with education in universities.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
In this regard I can think of several, including Atomic Energy of Canada. We also have federal forest research stations across Canada.
I am sure much can be done, for example in tree genetics, to assist some of the developing countries.
Last September when a group of us visited South America to participate in the Interparliamentary Conference at Lima, Peru, we were told that in various parts of Peru scientists had discovered several species of wood hitherto unknown. I agree with an earlier speaker in this debate who said that South America is certainly one place where a great deal of emphasis should be placed on assistance. It is only by helping people to help themselves that we are going to cure the social ills of other countries. Countries like the United States and other industrialized nations, regardless of financial wealth, cannot hope to provide all of the information and educational facilities required to assist the underdeveloped nations; the only way we can assist them is to help them to help themselves. This we can do through research programs of this type.
The humanitarian aspects of this bill have been mentioned and they are indeed very important. I think anyone who has visited South America and other countries of the world, where there is poverty, will realize that through research we can better their conditions. We must give these countries a plan and the trained personnel to solve their problems, and it is for this purpose that we require financial resources. In proceeding in this way and reaching solutions of this kind, we will be spending our money wisely.
In the Middle Ages scientists in the world did not gather together very often. Only recently have the best scientists of Europe and North America gathered together at the international level. In the old days scientists
DEBATES	2265
International Development Research Centre jealously guarded their knowledge; today the results of research in one country is almost straight-away passed on to scientists of other nations. This is one of the main purposes of this bill, and it would not be possible to put a bill like this into operation were this not the case.
This bill also breaks new ground in the field of international affairs by making provision for people from other developing countries of the world to sit on the board of governors. I think this is an excellent road on which to start out. While the majority of the board of governors will be Canadians, which I think is only right since Canada is providing the program, it is interesting to note that finally we are permitting people from other countries, who know their own problems firsthand, to sit on the board of governors of the International Development Research Centre of Canada. This is a step that will make the research program more effective. We will know the problems we have to face, the solutions we must work toward, and we will know the local conditions within which they must be applied.
I was pleased to hear the minister state in his speech that $30 million would be directed toward this plan over the first five years of operation. Although much of this $30 million is going to be spent in Canada, the nations we are assisting directly, with the balance of this money, will still benefit from this expenditure in Canada. This is a joint agreement. It is a plan whereby we will be solving our own problems both industrially and economically as well as solving similar problems in other coun tries.
I was astounded to learn that in the past only $1 out of every $200-I believe that is the correct figure one-half of one per cent- that was spent on foreign aid, has been directed toward foreign research aid programs. I think we have now come to realize that we could not continue to spend so little on research because we do not know whether our foreign aid program is being properly directed, and is actually solving problems in recipient countries. In fact, there have been times when past governments of Canada have not looked very seriously at this question of finding out how much good has been done by money spent in developing countries.
This bill starts us off on a new and very enlightened approach. Not only will we obtain first hand knowledge of problems existing in developing countries as a result of close relations with the representatives of other nations
January 12, 1970
2266	COMMONS DEBATES
International Development Research Centre on the board of governors, but we are also going to work together in research programs in order to find a plan to meet those problems and thereby help those nations to develop their economies. I think this in turn cannot help but build a better scientific and technological core, and hence a wider middle class society in developing countries.
As some of the members of this House have seen for themselves, one of the big problems in developing countries in the world today is that there are the two extremes: you have the very rich and the extremely poor. Developing a middle class society in such countries will give greater stability, and hence a better standard of living will result.
It is estimated that by the year 2000, 80 per cent of the world's population will live in those countries that today are classified as developing nations. One thing that we as a nation must strive toward is a plan to prepare the people of developing countries to look after themselves relatively well by the year 2000. I say this because if 80 per cent of the people of the world are still living in countries where they do not have enough to eat, proper clothing and the comforts of life, then we cannot help but have international problems that stem directly from such economic and social conditions.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I hope other countries in the world will follow this example and set up new agencies with a board of governors of an international character. I hope these agencies will go to work in this field of research as problem solving agencies. We in this Parliament must not only attack the problems of today. We must always attack those problems, but when we face a serious situation such as the suggestion that 80 per cent of the world's population faces possible poverty by the year 2000, we must look beyond today's horizon and do something constructive.
In this respect, I should like to give my full support and the support of a very interested group in my constituency. They support and congratulate the minister and his staff on the passage and implementation of this legislation. I am very pleased by the great interest of the Science Association of Deep River. The several hundred professional scientists and technological people in that association are interested in doing all they can to assist the government to implement this plan.

We also have a forest research station at Chalk River. This staff is extremely interested in providing assistance where it is needed in the field of forest genetics and other scientific projects. I know I speak for them when I say to the minister that he can count on the wholehearted support of this large body of scientific and technological people. I wish the minister and his staff every success in the implementation of this measure.
If there are things about this measure that must be revised in years to come, we should not hesitate to make changes which will make the plan more workable. No one group could bring in legislation of this far-reaching type that is 100 per cent efficient. This measure is certainly off to a flying start and I am sure that members on all sides of this House will agree that if in years to come changes are necessary, the government will meet with the same co-operative attitude which exists at this time.
In closing, let me once again compliment the minister and his staff on this far-reaching legislation. I compliment the government in general for the international character of the board of governors. This is a new plan that we hope will provide for more efficient spending of the money provided to assist the developing countries of this world. By the year 2000 we will be in a position to say that at least Canadians have done something useful to create peace in the world. We have taken the humanitarian and economic steps necessary to provide the people of developing countries with the mental tools to look after themselves.
